title: Intermediate Representations
summary: The seam between front end and back end: why compilers lower an AST into three-address code, control-flow graphs, and SSA form before optimizing, instead of optimizing the tree directly.

slides.markdown:
[asts-and-semantic-analysis](asts-and-semantic-analysis) leaves you with an annotated AST — structurally valid, type-checked, every name resolved. You could, in principle, go straight from that tree to machine code. Almost nothing does, and this topic is about why.

An IR (Intermediate Representation) is a deliberately neutral form sitting between the front end (language-specific) and the back end (target-specific): **three-address code** flattens nested expressions into simple, uniform instructions; **control-flow graphs** organize those instructions into blocks and jumps; **SSA form** adds one more constraint — every variable assigned exactly once — that makes a huge class of optimizations dramatically easier to write correctly.

This is the seam that makes LLVM's "many languages, one back end" model work, and it's the stage every optimization pass and every code generator actually operates on — not the AST, and not the raw machine code.

slides.sectionTitle: Why an IR exists at all
slides.markdown:
An AST's shape is dictated by the source language's grammar — nested expressions, language-specific control-flow constructs. Machine code's shape is dictated by one specific target's instruction set. Neither is a good place to write an optimization pass, because a pass written against one source language's AST shape doesn't transfer to a different language, and a pass written against one target's instructions doesn't transfer to a different CPU.

An IR breaks that coupling by belonging to neither side: it's flat and uniform enough that a front end for any source language can lower to it, and abstract enough (not yet committed to specific registers or specific target instructions) that any back end can consume it. Optimizations get written once, against the IR's shape, and every front end and every back end benefits — this is the direct mechanical reason LLVM lets Clang, `rustc`, and Swift share one optimizer and one set of code generators.

slides.subTitle: Flattening nested expressions
slides.markdown:
**Three-address code** is an IR shape where every instruction has at most one operator and at most three operands (typically: destination, and two sources) — no nesting. `x = (a + b) * (c - d)` becomes a short sequence:

```text
t1 = a + b
t2 = c - d
x  = t1 * t2
```

Every intermediate result gets its own **temporary** (`t1`, `t2`). This flattening is what makes an expression tractable for later analysis: instead of reasoning about an arbitrarily deep nested tree, every operation is now a uniform, simple statement, and a pass can walk the instruction sequence linearly instead of recursing through tree structure.

slides.sectionTitle: An AST lowered into a control-flow graph
slides.markdown:
![AST for an if/else versus its control-flow graph of basic blocks](assets/ast-vs-cfg.svg)

A **basic block** is a maximal sequence of instructions with exactly one entry point and one exit point — no jumps into the middle, no jumps out except at the very end. The **control-flow graph** is basic blocks as nodes and possible jumps between them as edges. This is the structure optimizations actually reason about: "can execution reach this block from that one" is a graph-reachability question once you're at this level, not a tree-traversal question.

slides.sectionTitle: Basic blocks: the unit optimizations reason about
slides.markdown:
The reason basic blocks matter as a concept, not just a diagramming convenience: within one block, execution is guaranteed to run every instruction in order, with no branching possible in the middle. That guarantee is exactly what makes **local** optimizations (ones that only need to reason about one block) simple and safe — common subexpression elimination within a block doesn't have to worry about some other code path skipping past the computation it's relying on, because by definition nothing branches into the middle of a block.

**Global** optimizations (across multiple blocks) need the control-flow graph's edges too, to know which blocks can reach which — that's exactly the information a tree or a flat instruction list without block boundaries doesn't give you for free.

slides.sectionTitle: SSA: every variable assigned exactly once
slides.markdown:
**Static Single Assignment (SSA)** form adds one more rule on top of three-address code: every variable is assigned exactly once in the program text. If your source code reassigns a variable multiple times, SSA form renames each assignment to a fresh version — `x1`, `x2`, `x3` — instead of reusing `x`.

Why this helps: in SSA, a variable's single assignment *is* its definition, so "where does this value come from" is answered by construction — there's no need to trace backward through possibly-reassigned code to figure out which assignment a given use actually refers to. This single property is what makes a huge fraction of modern optimization algorithms — constant propagation, dead code elimination, and more — dramatically simpler to state and implement correctly than the equivalent analysis on non-SSA code.

slides.sectionTitle: SSA before and after, with a phi node
Why a phi node shows up here
slides.markdown:
The direct answer to "why would a compiler introduce a phi node here": whenever a variable has more than one possible definition reaching the same use, and those definitions come from different predecessor blocks in the control-flow graph, SSA needs exactly one construct to represent "the value depends on which path was taken" while still keeping every variable single-assigned.

A phi node always sits at the start of a block that has multiple incoming edges (a **merge point**) — never inside a block with one predecessor, because there's no ambiguity to resolve there. Loops are the other common trigger: a loop variable updated each iteration needs a phi node right at the loop's entry block, merging "the initial value from before the loop" and "the updated value from the end of the previous iteration" — which is exactly why SSA-based optimizers reason about loops as a specific, recognizable graph shape (a back edge into a block with a phi) rather than needing special-case loop logic.

The temptation for a first-time compiler writer: skip the IR and try to run optimizations directly on the AST, since the tree is already there and lowering feels like extra work. This goes badly for a specific, recurring reason — the AST's nested, tree-shaped structure doesn't expose the things optimizations actually need: which values flow between which operations across control-flow boundaries, and whether a given definition is the *only* one reaching a particular use.

Common subexpression elimination on a raw AST means somehow reasoning about "is this subtree computed elsewhere" across arbitrary tree shapes and, worse, across branches and loops the tree structure doesn't flatten for you. On three-address code plus a control-flow graph, the same optimization is comparing linear instruction sequences within and across basic blocks — a fundamentally easier shape of problem, which is exactly why every serious optimizing compiler lowers first.

| | Stack-based (JVM bytecode) | Register/SSA-based (LLVM IR) |
|---|---|---|
| Operand model | Implicit — instructions push/pop a stack | Explicit — every instruction names its operands and destination |
| Compactness | Very compact bytecode | Larger, more verbose representation |
| Optimization friendliness | Harder — stack positions obscure data flow | Easier — SSA form makes data flow explicit by construction |
| Typical use | Portable bytecode for a VM to interpret/JIT | Ahead-of-time and JIT optimizing compiler middle-ends |

The JVM's bytecode optimizes for compactness and portability across the network/disk, then does most of its heavy optimization *after* converting to a more analysis-friendly internal form inside the JIT — depth on this specific split lives in the `runtimes` group's coverage of bytecode VMs. This topic's IR (three-address, SSA) is the shape optimizing compilers actually reason with internally, regardless of what format ships to disk.

Every optimization pass in [compiler-optimizations](compiler-optimizations) — constant folding, dead code elimination, common subexpression elimination, loop transformations — is written against exactly the representation this topic built: three-address instructions, organized into basic blocks and a control-flow graph, in SSA form. That's not a coincidence; it's the entire reason this lowering step exists.

The uniformity payoff compounds: a pass doesn't need special cases for "this came from a for-loop" versus "this came from a while-loop" — by the time it's IR, both are just blocks and edges. That's the concrete leverage a good IR design buys, and it's worth more than it looks on first read.

This topic covered the *shape* of the IR — how it's structured so analysis is tractable. [compiler-optimizations](compiler-optimizations) covers what actually gets *done* with that shape: the specific passes that turn correct-but-naive IR into fast IR. [code-generation](code-generation) covers the other direction — turning that same IR into real target instructions, once optimization is done with it.

Both of the next two topics assume this one: "the IR is in SSA form, organized into a control-flow graph of basic blocks" is the starting assumption for everything that follows in this group's back-end coverage.
